# Dispatch: lane L15 of the representation wave (0004): Verifier internals: the owned stage and uses read the flow edges

This file is your whole assignment. The packet it quotes is `proposals/0004-representation/README.md`. Read the owner's guideline below in full before anything else: every hunk you write is judged by it.

## The owner's guideline: representation first

Read every word of this section before your first edit, and again before
your handoff. It is the owner's, it is how every hunk of this wave is judged,
and it binds harder than any convenience. The operational form comes first;
the full source document follows it, verbatim, and you read that too.

### How it binds in this wave

- **Before every branch, flag, guard, `Maybe`, `optional`, `bool`, sentinel
  string, "unknown" arm, internal-error case or `if` you add, stop and ask:
  what representation would make this state impossible?** Change the data,
  the type, or the invariant first, within your exclusive writes. Add the
  branch only when the case is essential (the problem has it, not the
  representation), and say so in the comment above it.
- **Parse at the boundary, once.** A check whose result is thrown away
  (a `bool` returned, a `LogicalResult` with the fact discarded, a string
  compared and dropped) is a validator: return a type or value that carries
  what was learned, and delete every downstream re-check it makes redundant.
- **Every string that names a thing is a missing type.** A string key, a
  printed name used as an identity, a kind written as text, a role or
  category spelled in prose: make it an enum, a typed identity, or a
  generated table, unless it is text for a human or the format MLIR prints.
- **A switch on a tag is a polymorphism not yet named.** If you add a case to
  a switch in more than one place, move the variation into data (a table, a
  trait, an ODS field, a record of functions) and dispatch once.
- **One fact, one place.** A fact held twice (in a type and an attribute, in
  C++ and in Idris, in a test and in the code under test) is generated from
  its one source or deleted.
- **Special cases are coordinate errors until proven essential.** Before you
  write "except when", look for the coordinate (half-open range, a sentinel,
  an index instead of a name, a total order) under which the exception is
  the rule.
- **Delete what the representation makes dead in the same change**: the
  guard it obviates, the error branch that can no longer fire, the test that
  checked the impossible state. A representation added beside its
  predecessor is a second copy, not a fix.
- **The limit (Brooks).** Do not force two genuinely different cases into one
  representation; that hides the branch in a flag. Representation removes
  accidental complexity, never essential complexity. When you keep a branch,
  it is because the problem has two cases.
- **Your handoff states it.** For each obligation, one line: the state made
  unrepresentable, the check moved to a boundary, or the branch deleted; or
  the reason the case is essential. A hunk that adds control flow and names
  none of these is sent back.

### The source document (its text verbatim, its headings nested under this section)

#### Purpose

To document and ground one principle: the biggest lever in programming is the data representation, not the control flow. When a new case shows up, you can patch the trace of the computation with another branch, flag, or guard — and complexity piles up in the control flow. Or you can change the data, types, and invariants so the case stops being special, or stops being expressible at all. Brooks, Pike, Raymond, and Torvalds have said this in almost the same words across fifty years, and type theory explains why it works.

##### In Scope

- The practitioner lineage and its explicit chain of citation: Brooks → Pike → Raymond → Torvalds.
- Why precise types remove branches: illegal states, parsing vs. validation, null, parametricity.
- Named techniques that remove branches: polymorphic dispatch, choosing coordinates, sentinel nodes, reifying control flow as data.
- The limit: where representation costs more than it saves, and the essential-vs-accidental complexity line.

##### Out of Scope

- Treating this as an AI topic. The sources run 1975–2019 and predate it entirely.
- Paradigm advocacy. The principle holds in C, OCaml, TypeScript, and Lisp alike.
- A refactoring how-to. Patterns appear only as evidence.
- Performance benchmarking. Indirection cost is noted as a limit, not measured.

#### DOK 4: Spiky Points of View (SPOVs)

- **Spiky POV 1: The data representation determines a program’s complexity. The algorithm and the control flow are downstream of it.**
   - **Elaboration:** Code review argues about control flow, interviews test algorithms, and “clean code” is taught as the art of writing better conditionals. The lineage says the leverage is upstream of all of that, in the shape of the data — and it says so in nearly identical words from Brooks to Torvalds (Insights 1, 2, 3). What makes the claim more than one school’s taste is the convergence: four respected practitioners reached it independently across thirty-one years, and two of them cite Brooks by name (Insight 10). The practical consequence is an ordering. When complexity grows, change the representation before you add to the control flow, because the representation is where the complexity actually lives.
- **Spiky POV 2: Most of the branches in typical code are not handling the problem. They are guarding against states a more precise representation would have made impossible.**
   - **Elaboration:** Three independent booleans — `loading`, `error`, `data` — admit eight states, of which only a few are valid; the rest get guarded against everywhere the value travels. A four-case sum type admits exactly four, all valid, and the guards have nothing left to guard (Insight 4). Minsky’s name for the move is “make illegal states unrepresentable.” Alexis King sharpens it: validation checks a condition and throws away what it learned, so every caller downstream must check again, while parsing returns a type that carries the proof, so the check happens once at the boundary (Insight 6). Null is the proof by counterexample — it sits in every type at once, which is exactly why it forces a check on every use (Insight 5). The day-to-day implication: when you reach for a guard, the better question is usually not “is this branch right?” but “what representation would make this state impossible?”
- **Spiky POV 3: Most special cases belong to the representation, not the problem. Change the representation and they are gone, not handled.**
   - **Elaboration:** Special cases are usually treated as inherent and met with more code. They often are not inherent. Dijkstra’s half-open interval makes length equal `b − a`, the empty range clean, and adjacent ranges gap-free — the off-by-one is not handled, it is unrepresentable (Insight 11). Homogeneous coordinates turn translation from an affine exception into the same matrix multiply as rotation, as a matter of arithmetic (Insight 12). A sentinel node makes the first and last elements stop being special by giving the boundary a real node (Insight 8). None of these changed the algorithm; they changed the coordinate system, and the special case vanished. The ceiling of the move is to turn tangled control flow into data — an AST with a small evaluator — with Greenspun’s rule as the warning that a complex enough program grows a bad interpreter by accident if you don’t build a good one on purpose (Insights 13, 14).

#### Experts

- **Fred Brooks** — Turing Award winner; managed IBM’s System/360; wrote *The Mythical Man-Month*. Originated “representation is the essence of programming” and the essential-vs-accidental complexity split. He is the source of the whole lineage and of the limit that keeps it honest. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month) · [Wikiquote](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Fred_Brooks)
- **Rob Pike** — Bell Labs (Unix, UTF-8, Plan 9), co-creator of Go. His Rule 5, “data dominates,” is the cleanest operational form of Brooks and cites him by page — the documented second link in the chain. [Notes on Programming in C](https://zoo.cs.yale.edu/classes/cs323/doc/Pike.pdf) · [cat-v archive](http://doc.cat-v.org/bell_labs/pikestyle)
- **Eric S. Raymond** — Author of *The Cathedral and the Bazaar*. His “smart data structures and dumb code” came from replacing fetchmail’s protocol branching with a method table, and he attributes it to Brooks directly. [Cathedral and the Bazaar §6](http://www.catb.org/esr/writings/cathedral-bazaar/cathedral-bazaar/ar01s06.html)
- **Linus Torvalds** — Created Linux and Git. His 2006 note, “good programmers worry about data structures and their relationships,” is the principle from someone who built two data-structure-first systems at scale. [LWN archive](https://lwn.net/Articles/193245/)
- **Yaron Minsky** — Head of Technology at Jane Street; industrial OCaml advocate. Coined “make illegal states unrepresentable,” the mechanism behind SPOV 2. [Effective ML talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-J8YyfrSwTk) · [Effective ML Revisited](https://blog.janestreet.com/effective-ml-revisited/) · [OCaml for the Masses](https://plv.mpi-sws.org/plerg/papers/minsky-ocaml-masses.pdf)
- **Alexis King** — Functional programming writer (Haskell, Racket). “Parse, Don’t Validate” is the sharpest practical form of the mechanism: a parser returns a type that carries its proof, so the check happens once. [Parse, don’t validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/)
- **C.A.R. (Tony) Hoare** — Turing Award winner; invented Quicksort and Hoare logic. His “billion-dollar mistake” talk is the counterexample that proves the mechanism: null lives in every type, so it forces a check everywhere. [InfoQ talk](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/Null-References-The-Billion-Dollar-Mistake-Tony-Hoare/)
- **Philip Wadler** — Edinburgh; co-designed Haskell type classes. “Theorems for Free!” shows a polymorphic type signature alone constrains what the code can do. [Edinburgh](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/theorems-for-free/) · [source](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/free/free.ps)
- **John C. Reynolds** — Co-discovered parametric polymorphism (System F). His Abstraction Theorem proves well-typed polymorphic code cannot branch on a concrete representation — the floor beneath Wadler. [CMU exposition](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rwh/courses/chtt/pdfs/reynolds.pdf) · [reproduction](https://github.com/ionathanch/parapoly)
- **Edsger W. Dijkstra** — Turing Award winner; structured programming. EWD831 is the cleanest “choose your coordinates” case: the half-open interval makes off-by-one unrepresentable. [EWD831](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/transcriptions/EWD08xx/EWD831.html) · [archive](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/)
- **Abelson & Sussman** — Wrote SICP (MIT 6.001). Chapter 4 is the ceiling of the principle: reify control flow as data and write an evaluator. [SICP Ch. 4](https://sarabander.github.io/sicp/html/Chapter-4.xhtml) · [PDF](https://web.mit.edu/6.001/6.037/sicp.pdf)
- **Martin Fowler** — Wrote *Refactoring*. “Replace Conditional with Polymorphism” is the named transform from control flow to data dispatch. [Catalog](https://refactoring.com/catalog/replaceConditionalWithPolymorphism.html) · [editions](https://martinfowler.com/articles/refactoring-2nd-changes.html)
- **Bobby Woolf** — Patterns author. The Null Object pattern represents absence as an object, removing null-checks wholesale. [Null Object paper](http://www.cs.uni.edu/~wallingf/patterns/elementary/papers/null-object.pdf)

#### DOK 3: Insights

Conclusions drawn from the sources below; the bridge from raw material to the SPOVs.

##### The lineage

- **Insight 1 — Two ways to absorb a new case.** Patch the trace (a branch, flag, or guard) and complexity gathers in the control flow; change the structure (data, types, invariants) and the case stops being special or expressible. Same problem, two surfaces, opposite cost profiles.
- **Insight 2 — Brooks stated it; Pike made it operational.** Brooks’ line sits under a heading that reads “Representation Is the Essence of Programming,” next to “strategic breakthrough will come from redoing the representation of your data.” Pike’s Rule 5 — “data dominates… the algorithms will almost always be self-evident” — is the same claim with a working edge, and his “(See Brooks p. 102.)” is a literal citation.
- **Insight 3 — It holds at the largest scale.** Torvalds credits Git’s success to designing code around the data. Git’s content-addressed object model and the Linux data structures are existence proofs, not toy examples.
- **Insight 10 — The convergence is the evidence.** Brooks (1975) → Pike (1989, citing Brooks) → Raymond (1997, calling it “the same point”) → Torvalds (2006, independent), across four subcultures with the citations written down. That is what separates a real principle from a fashion.

##### Why precise types remove branches

- **Insight 4 — Illegal states are the hidden source of branching.** Three independent flags give eight states, few of them valid; the invalid ones get guarded everywhere. A sum type gives exactly the valid states, so the guards have nothing to guard. That is what “make illegal states unrepresentable” buys.
- **Insight 5 — Null is the mechanism, inverted.** Null is effectively a member of every type, which is precisely why it forces a check on every dereference. It is the worst possible representation, and the fix Hoare already knew and skipped — the disjoint union — is the sum type.
- **Insight 6 — Validation discards proof; parsing keeps it.** A validator returns nothing and forces every downstream caller to re-check. A parser returns a refined type that carries the proof, so the check happens once at the boundary and never again. This is the most precise account of how a representation removes control flow: the information the branch tested for moves into the type.
- **Insight 9 — A type signature is an enforced specification.** Wadler’s free theorems and Reynolds’ Abstraction Theorem show a polymorphic signature alone constrains behavior — `∀a. [a] → [a]` can only rearrange, duplicate, or drop, never inspect or invent — and that well-typed clients cannot branch on a concrete representation. The type is a machine-checked constraint, not a comment.

##### Techniques that remove branches

- **Insight 7 — A switch on a type tag is a polymorphism not yet named.** Fowler’s refactoring moves the same variation from a tag plus branches into object identity plus dispatch. The variation didn’t leave; it moved into the data.
- **Insight 8 — Absence and boundaries are representational choices.** A null object represents “nothing” as a real object, deleting every null-check. A sentinel node represents the list boundary as a real node, so first-and-last stop being special — CLRS even shows a sentinel removing a per-iteration loop test. One added object removes a category of branches.
- **Insight 11 — Off-by-one is usually a coordinate error.** The half-open interval is the one convention where length is `b − a`, the empty range is clean, and adjacent ranges share a boundary cleanly. The error isn’t fixed; the coordinate system makes it impossible.
- **Insight 12 — Some special cases are pure coordinate artifacts.** Translation is an affine exception in Cartesian coordinates but the same matrix multiply as rotation in homogeneous ones. The exception lived in the representation, provably, not the problem.
- **Insight 13 — Greenspun’s rule is the principle as a warning.** Deny yourself good representational tools and complexity grows you a bad interpreter by accident. At scale you build the representation deliberately or accrete it badly.
- **Insight 14 — The ceiling is to make control flow into data.** SICP’s “the evaluator is just another program” is the senior-most form: represent the logic as an AST or transition table and write a small evaluator. Table-driven code, state machines, and DSLs are one family — branching pushed out of code into inspectable data.

##### The limit

- **Insight 15 — Representation is globally cheap but locally expensive; control flow is the reverse.** A representation costs design, abstraction, indirection, and sometimes speed up front. A branch is free now and expensive later, through drift and combinatorial state. That cost structure, not virtue, is why adding a branch is the common reflex and investing in representation is the experienced one.
- **Insight 16 — It removes accidental complexity, not essential complexity.** Brooks’ line is the boundary. Representation collapses accidental special cases but cannot dissolve essential ones; force two genuinely different cases into one representation and the branching just hides inside config flags. The right representation is usually only visible after the imperative version exposes the pattern, so part of the skill is knowing when the refactor is earned.

##### Category 1: The practitioner lineage

- **Source 1: Fred Brooks, *The Mythical Man-Month*, Ch. 9 (1975)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “Show me your flowcharts and conceal your tables, and I shall continue to be mystified. Show me your tables, and I won’t usually need your flowcharts; they’ll be obvious.”
      - Ch. 9, “Ten Pounds in a Five-Pound Sack,” p. 102; same page in the 1975 first edition and 1995 Anniversary Edition.
      - Sits under the subsection “Representation Is the Essence of Programming,” after: “strategic breakthrough will come from redoing the representation of your data or table. This is where the heart of a program lies.”
      - Brooks wrote “flowcharts” (plural); the singular version that circulates is Raymond’s paraphrase.
   - **Summary:** The deepest gains come from rethinking the data, not from cleverness in the code. The first articulation of the principle.
   - **Link:** [PDF](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~weimerw/2018-481/readings/mythical-man-month.pdf) · [Wikiquote](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Fred_Brooks)
- **Source 2: Rob Pike, “Notes on Programming in C” (Feb 21, 1989)**
   - **Facts:**
      - Rule 5: “Data dominates. If you’ve chosen the right data structures and organized things well, the algorithms will almost always be self-evident. Data structures, not algorithms, are central to programming. (See Brooks p. 102.)”
      - Later section “Programming with data”: algorithms “can often be encoded compactly, efficiently and expressively as data rather than, say, as lots of if statements.”
      - Internal Bell Labs document, never formally published. Rule 6: “There is no Rule 6.”

   - **Facts:**
      - Lesson 9 of 19: “Smart data structures and dumb code works a lot better than the other way around.”
      - Followed by: “Brooks, Chapter 9… Allowing for thirty years of terminological/cultural shift, it’s the same point.”
      - He reached it by replacing fetchmail’s monolithic protocol branching with a table of method pointers (POP2/POP3/IMAP). Book: O’Reilly, 1999.
   - **Summary:** A field-tested instance plus an explicit attribution to Brooks.
   - **Link:** [catb.org §6](http://www.catb.org/esr/writings/cathedral-bazaar/cathedral-bazaar/ar01s06.html)
- **Source 4: Linus Torvalds, git mailing list (Jul 27, 2006)**
   - **Facts:**

      - Body: “I’m a huge proponent of designing your code around the data, rather than the other way around… one of the reasons git has been fairly successful.”
      - Thread “Re: Licensing and the library version of git.” Correct date is July 27, 2006; many sites wrongly say June 27.
   - **Summary:** Independent corroboration from the builder of Linux and Git, crediting Git’s success to data-first design.
   - **Link:** [LWN archive](https://lwn.net/Articles/193245/)

##### Category 2: Why precise types remove branches

- **Source 5: Yaron Minsky, “Effective ML” / “Effective ML Revisited” (2010/2011)**
   - **Facts:**
      - Coined “make illegal states unrepresentable” in a 2010 Harvard CS51 lecture; it appears as a section heading in the 2011 Jane Street blog post.
      - The `connection_info` example: a flat record of nullable fields refactored into a sum type where each state carries only its legal fields.
      - “OCaml for the Masses” (ACM, 2011): “Now that the invariants are part of the types, the compiler can detect and reject code that would violate these invariants.”
      - The slogan is verbatim in the talk and blog, not in the ACM article body (same code example, though).
   - **Summary:** Put invariants in the type and the compiler rejects illegal states for free, removing the checks that would guard them.
   - **Link:** [talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-J8YyfrSwTk) · [blog](https://blog.janestreet.com/effective-ml-revisited/) · [PDF](https://plv.mpi-sws.org/plerg/papers/minsky-ocaml-masses.pdf)
- **Source 6: Alexis King, “Parse, Don’t Validate” (Nov 5, 2019)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “`parseNonEmpty` gives the caller access to the information it learned, while `validateNonEmpty` just throws it away.”
      - `validateNonEmpty` returns `()`; `parseNonEmpty` returns `NonEmpty a`, “a refinement of the input type that preserves the knowledge gained in the type system.”
      - “once those checks have been performed, they never need to be checked again.”
      - Names “shotgun parsing” (LangSec, 2016) and builds explicitly on Minsky.
   - **Summary:** Validation discards proof and forces re-checks; parsing carries proof in the type so the check happens once at the boundary.
   - **Link:** [Parse, don’t validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/)
- **Source 7: C.A.R. Hoare, “Null References: The Billion Dollar Mistake” (QCon London, 2009)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “I call it my billion-dollar mistake. It was the invention of the null reference in 1965… I couldn’t resist the temptation to put in a null reference, simply because it was so easy to implement.”
      - Added null to ALGOL W while designing the first comprehensive reference type system; the alternative he skipped was “discrimination of objects belonging to a disjoint union class.”
      - Null is effectively in every type, so a check is required on every use. Year is 1965 (an InfoQ note saying 1964 is wrong).
   - **Summary:** Null is the worst representation — a quasi-illegal state in every type at once, forcing branches everywhere. The mechanism proven backwards.
   - **Link:** [QCon abstract](https://qconlondon.com/london-2009/qconlondon.com/london-2009/presentation/Null+References_+The+Billion+Dollar+Mistake.html) · [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/Null-References-The-Billion-Dollar-Mistake-Tony-Hoare/)
- **Source 8: Philip Wadler, “Theorems for Free!” (FPCA ’89)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “From the type of a polymorphic function we can derive a theorem that it satisfies. Every function of the same type satisfies the same theorem.”
      - `∀a. [a] → [a]` can only rearrange, duplicate, or drop elements — not inspect or invent them.
      - Credits Reynolds’ abstraction theorem. FPCA ’89, ACM, pp. 347–359, DOI 10.1145/99370.99404.
   - **Summary:** A polymorphic signature alone is a proof-carrying spec that rules out classes of implementations.
   - **Link:** [Edinburgh](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/theorems-for-free/) · [source](https://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/free/free.ps)
- **Source 9: John C. Reynolds, “Types, Abstraction and Parametric Polymorphism” (IFIP 1983)**
   - **Facts:**
      - The Abstraction Theorem: clients of an abstract type are polymorphic and “enjoy stability properties across changes of representation determined entirely by their types.”
      - Well-typed polymorphic clients cannot distinguish two implementations related by a representation relation — they cannot branch on the concrete representation.
      - *Information Processing 83*, North-Holland, pp. 513–523. Co-foundational with Girard’s System F.
   - **Summary:** The type discipline forces uniform behavior across representations; branching on representation is provably impossible. The floor beneath Wadler.
   - **Link:** [CMU](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rwh/courses/chtt/pdfs/reynolds.pdf) · [reproduction](https://github.com/ionathanch/parapoly)

##### Category 3: Techniques that remove branches

- **Source 10: Martin Fowler, “Replace Conditional with Polymorphism,” *Refactoring* (1999/2018)**
   - **Facts:**
      - A `switch (bird.type)` returning per-type behavior becomes subclasses each implementing `plumage()`.
      - 1st ed. p. 255; 2nd ed. p. 272. Upstream step: “Replace Type Code with Subclasses” (2nd ed. p. 362).
   - **Summary:** The same variation moves from tag-plus-branches into identity-plus-dispatch; the conditional becomes one virtual call.
   - **Link:** [catalog](https://refactoring.com/catalog/replaceConditionalWithPolymorphism.html) · [editions](https://martinfowler.com/articles/refactoring-2nd-changes.html)
- **Source 11: Bobby Woolf, “The Null Object Pattern,” *PLoPD3* (1996/1998)**
   - **Facts:**
      - Intent: “Provide a surrogate for another object that shares the same interface but does nothing.”
      - Without it, callers must “check its controller before sending those messages… All of this conditional code would clutter the view’s implementation.”
      - In *Pattern Languages of Program Design 3*, Addison-Wesley, pp. 5–18. Folded into Fowler as “Introduce Null Object,” later “Introduce Special Case.”
   - **Summary:** Represent absence as a no-op object and every null-check disappears. Absence is a representational choice.
   - **Link:** [paper](http://www.cs.uni.edu/~wallingf/patterns/elementary/papers/null-object.pdf) · [ACM DL](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/273448.273450)
- **Source 12: Edsger W. Dijkstra, EWD831, “Why Numbering Should Start at Zero” (Aug 11, 1982)**
   - **Facts:**
      - Of four interval conventions, prefers lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive `[a, b)`.
      - Excluding the lower bound forces it “into the realm of the unnatural numbers” at the smallest natural number; including the upper bound does the same for the empty sequence. Only `[a, b)` avoids both.
      - Gives zero-based indexing the “nicer range 0 ≤ i < N.” Mesa at Xerox PARC found the other conventions “a constant source of clumsiness and mistakes.”
   - **Summary:** The half-open interval makes length `b − a`, the empty range clean, and adjacent ranges gap-free. Off-by-one becomes unrepresentable, not handled.
   - **Link:** [EWD831](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/transcriptions/EWD08xx/EWD831.html) · [PDF](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/ewd08xx/EWD831.PDF)
- **Source 13: Sentinel Nodes — CLRS, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd ed. (2009)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “A sentinel is a dummy object that allows us to simplify boundary conditions.” A circular doubly linked list uses a sentinel `L.nil` between head and tail.
      - §10.2, pp. 236–241. Exercise 10.2-4 (p. 240): set `L.nil.key = k` and the sentinel is a guaranteed match, removing the per-iteration `x ≠ L.nil` test.
   - **Summary:** A dummy boundary node merges the edge case into the normal path. One node removes a category of branches.
   - **Link:** [Rutgers Ch.10](https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~ajl213/CLRS/Ch10.pdf) · [algs4](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu)
- **Source 14: Homogeneous Coordinates — Foley, van Dam, Feiner & Hughes, *Computer Graphics: Principles and Practice*, 2nd ed. (1996)**
   - **Facts:**
      - In Cartesian coordinates, translation `(x', y') = (x + tx, y + ty)` is affine, not linear, so it cannot be a 2×2 matrix multiply, unlike rotation and scaling.
      - Representing `(x, y)` as `(x, y, 1)` makes translation a 3×3 matrix multiply, uniform with the rest; in 3D, 4×4 matrices give one pipeline.
      - Ch. 5, pp. 201–226. Drexel CS536 slides (citing Foley/van Dam): “Homogeneous coordinates: allows all transformations to be treated as matrix multiplications.”
   - **Summary:** The translation special case is an artifact of the Cartesian representation; the homogeneous one removes it as arithmetic.
   - **Link:** [Drexel slides](https://www.cs.drexel.edu/~deb39/Classes/CS536/Lectures/L-18_Transformations.pdf) · [Brown record](https://cs.brown.edu/people/jhughes/papers/vanDam-CGP-1995/main.htm)
- **Source 15: Abelson & Sussman, SICP, Ch. 4 “Metalinguistic Abstraction” (2nd ed., 1996)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “It is no exaggeration to regard this as the most fundamental idea in programming: The evaluator… is just another program.” (bold in original)
      - §4.1.5 “Data as Programs”: “our evaluator is seen to be a universal machine.”
      - Builds a metacircular evaluator — Lisp evaluated by a Lisp program. Ch. 4 p. 364; §4.1.5 p. 382.
   - **Summary:** When control flow gets hairy, represent it as data and write an evaluator. Table-driven code, state machines, and DSLs are one family.
   - **Link:** [SICP Ch. 4](https://sarabander.github.io/sicp/html/Chapter-4.xhtml) · [PDF](https://web.mit.edu/6.001/6.037/sicp.pdf)
- **Source 16: Greenspun’s Tenth Rule (c. 1993)**
   - **Facts:**
      - “Any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains an ad hoc, informally-specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of half of Common Lisp.”
      - Philip Greenspun, c. 1993; spread via USENET signatures; never formally published. “There aren’t 9 preceding laws. I was just trying to give the rule a memorable name.”
   - **Summary:** Without good representational tools, complexity grows a bad interpreter on its own. The inverse of SICP.
   - **Link:** [research page](https://philip.greenspun.com/research/) · [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenspun%27s_tenth_rule)

##### Category 4: The limit

- **Source 17: Fred Brooks, “No Silver Bullet” (1986/1995)**
   - **Facts:**
      - Splits *essential* complexity (inherent in the problem) from *accidental* complexity (introduced by tools and representations).
      - Appears in the 1995 Anniversary Edition of *The Mythical Man-Month*.
      - Representation can collapse accidental complexity but not essential complexity.
   - **Summary:** The boundary of the principle. It removes accidental special cases, not essential ones; forcing different cases into one representation just hides the branching. The right representation is often only clear after the imperative version exposes the pattern.
   - **Link:** [No Silver Bullet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Silver_Bullet) · [Mythical Man-Month](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month)

### ir-verify-11: `ownership::readFrom` re-derives from an isa ladder what the flow edges already declare

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Evidence | `Verify/Uses.cpp:56-72`: `FieldOp` gives its value, a `ViewLikeOpInterface` view its source, a `memref.load` of a counted element its buffer, a match's case argument its scrutinee. The flow edges declare the same reads: `FlowOps.cpp:110-114` (`FieldOp`: a part of the value, read, flows to the result), `:130-142` (`MatchOp`: a part of the scrutinee flows to each case argument), `:269-273` (`tensor.extract`). `memref.load` has no flow model. 15 files call `readFrom`, `viewRoot` or `isStatic`. |
| Counterexample | A new projecting op (for example a field read of a record column) declares its flow edge, and the owned walk still treats its result as made from nothing ("makes a value that holds references, which neither holds one of its own nor is read from a value that does") until someone adds an arm here. |
| Root cause | The decision of the representation wave (D7, "one account of how a value moves") was not carried into `readFrom`. It keeps its own list of projections. |
| Correction | `readFrom(v)` is the `of` value of the flow edge into `v` whose `from` is a `Part` of a `Whole` (read, not taken), from `flowEdgesOf` of `v`'s defining op or its region's owner. `memref.load` gets an external flow model (a part of the buffer's elements flows to the result), as `tensor.extract` has. `ViewLikeOpInterface` stays (upstream's). |
| Deletion | The `FieldOp`, `MatchOp` and `memref::LoadOp` arms. |
| Consumers | `lib/IR/Verify/Uses.cpp`, `FlowOps.cpp` (the memref.load model); readers whose answers must not change: `lib/Analysis/Ownership/{Borrows,Reuses,Values}.cpp`, `lib/Transforms/Ownership/{Classes,Placement,Reshape,Share}.cpp`, `lib/Transforms/Narrow/Facts.cpp`, `lib/Conversion/{Runtime,StaticData}.cpp`, `lib/Transforms/Expect/ResetsUnshared.cpp`. |
| Discriminator | A googletest box: for each op with a Part→Whole read edge, `readFrom(result)` is the edge's source. The owned-stage fixtures must not change. |
| Verification here | `make typecheck`. |
| Size and risk | About 15 lines out, 3 arms. Medium risk: every ownership reader leans on `readFrom`, and the new memref.load model is seen by Escapes and Exclusivity too. |
| Insight | 7, one fact one place |

### ir-verify-12: the owned stage's crossings into upstream's buffer ops are protocols of position and use count

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Evidence | `Verify/OwnedOps.cpp:94-106`: a counted element loaded by an upstream op must have one use, "the idr.dup right after it" (`op.getNextNode()`). `:36-39`, `:190-214`, `:233-243`: a fresh allocation's or an `idr.own.give`'s reference rides a plain value (`carry`) until an `idr.own.adopt` or a store takes it (`takesCarried`, `storedBy`). `Verify.h:159-161`: a `transit` set for "a reference their plain type cannot say". `OpsOwnership.cpp:120-139`: the adopt and give verifiers check the same pairs from the other side. |
| Counterexample | Any pass that puts an op between a `memref.load` and its `idr.dup` (a debug counter, a cast) makes the owned verifier refuse correct code. A reference in transit is a third kind of value the walk must test for at every use (`carried` appears in 7 functions). |
| Root cause | Upstream's memref ops take plain types, so each place a counted reference enters or leaves memory is split into an upstream op plus an op of ours. Their pairing is held by position and use count, not by an op. |
| Correction | idr-rc writes the three crossings as ops of ours: `idr.own.load` (load a counted element with a reference of its own), `idr.own.store` (store an owned element, which takes its reference) and `idr.own.alloc` (an owned buffer at once). Each lowers to the upstream op and the count operation, before upstream's memref lowering. |
| Deletion | `loaded()`'s adjacency rule; `carry`, `carried`, `transit`, `takesCarried`, `storedBy` and `make`'s allocation arm; `OwnAdoptOp`, `OwnGiveOp` and their verifiers. |
| Consumers | `include/idr/IR/IdrOwnershipOps.td`, `Verify.h`; `lib/IR/Verify/{Owned,OwnedOps}.cpp`, `OpsOwnership.cpp`, `FlowOps.cpp`; `lib/Transforms/Ownership/**` (idr-rc's placement and reshape, which today insert dup, adopt and give); `lib/Conversion/**` (lowering of the three ops). |
| Discriminator | Before: a fixture with an unrelated pure op between a counted load and its dup is refused. After: it cannot be written, and the owned fixtures over buffers verify. |
| Verification here | `make typecheck`. |
| Size and risk | About 90 lines out, one value role and 3 position rules. Medium to high risk: the bufferization handoff and idr-rc. Essential and kept: that upstream types hold no grade (`view` of a builtin buffer is plain, `upstreamHolds`). Only the pairing by position goes. |
| Insight | 4, 6 |

### ir-verify-18: the owned walk's view of a value is three overlapping predicates over three maps

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Evidence | `Verify/Owned.cpp:63-121` and `Verify.h:108-166`: `tracked` (owned and not static), `carried` (in `transit`), `isView` (counts, not owned, not static, not carried) and `alive`. They are kept in `held`, `transit` and `owners`, plus a `counted` cache. `ownership::isStatic` (`Verify/Uses.cpp:48-54`) walks a definition chain on every call, and `tracked`/`isView` are called at nearly every use (regrade 7 times, operands 3, `enter` 2, `ownersAcross` 2). |
| Counterexample | The predicates are disjoint only through their definitions' order (`isView` excludes `carried`, `tracked` excludes static). A reorder of the tests in `regrade` changes meaning, and nothing states which roles exist. |
| Root cause | A value's role in the walk (untracked, owned, in transit, a view of some owners) is a sum, computed again at each question. |
| Correction | `enum class Role { Untracked, Owned, Carried, View }`, decided once per value at its definition and memoized. The state is one `DenseMap<Value, Slot>` with `Slot = std::variant<Held{int}, Viewing{SmallVector<Value>}>`. (If ir-verify-12 lands, `Carried` goes too.) |
| Deletion | `transit`; the predicate chains (`switch (role)` at each site); the repeated `isStatic` walks. |
| Consumers | `include/idr/IR/Verify.h`; `lib/IR/Verify/{Owned,OwnedOps,OwnedRegions}.cpp`. |
| Discriminator | The owned fixtures (`tests/idr/ownership/**`, `tests/reduce-regions/owned*`) must not change. |
| Verification here | `make typecheck`. |
| Size and risk | About 30 lines out; few branches deleted (each role's arm is essential). Low to medium risk. Value is clarity and cost. |
| Insight | 4 |

| Counterexample | An edit that pushes onto one list in a loop that skips a knot misaligns the other two. `zip_equal` asserts only in debug. |
| Root cause | One knot's facts (its members, the array named, where it is reported) are spread over three vectors. |
| Correction | `struct Knot { SmallVector<unsigned> members; unsigned named; std::optional<Location> at; }`, with `knotOf` mapping to a `Knot *`. |
| Deletion | The three vectors and the pair-valued map. |
| Consumers | `lib/IR/Verify/Knots.cpp`. |
| Discriminator | `tests/reject/*cycle*` messages must not change. |
| Verification here | `make typecheck`. |

## Contracts you supply or consume (verbatim from README §4)

**S1. `idr::MatchOpInterface`** (ODS text by L05 in `IdrInterfaces.td`;
implementation and the base class by L01). Attached to `idr.match` and
`idr.match_lit` through `Idr_MatchOpBase`. Methods: `::mlir::Value
getScrutinee()`; `unsigned getNumCases()`; `::mlir::Region
&getCaseRegion(unsigned)`; `::mlir::Region &getDefaultRegion()`; `unsigned
caseOf(::mlir::Region &)` (a case region's index, asserted to be one of the
op's case regions); `std::optional<::idr::Tag> knownTag(::mlir::Region &)`
(the constructor a case region is entered at; none for the default and for
`idr.match_lit`); `::mlir::Operation *rebuild(::mlir::RewriterBase &,
::mlir::TypeRange results, ::llvm::ArrayRef<unsigned> keptCases,
::mlir::Region *defaultRegion)`. Builders (`skipDefaultBuilders = 1`):
`MatchOp(TypeRange results, Value scrutinee, ArrayRef<Tag> tags)` and
`MatchLitOp(TypeRange results, Value scrutinee, ArrayAttr cases)`, each
making an empty default and one empty region per key; a builder of a default
adds its block with `createBlock(&op.getDefaultRegion(), {},
{scrutinee.getType()}, {loc})`. Every reader of `getRegionNumber()` as a case
index goes through `caseOf` (`IdentitiesRecord.cpp:155,277,283`,
`OpsCon.cpp:284`, `Expect/Placement.cpp:63`, `Tail/WhileDo.cpp:170`), and
every reader of the default by number takes `getDefaultRegion()`
(`Asm.cpp:226`, `FlowOps.cpp:137`). The four `RegionBranchOpInterface`
members are written once in the base class. "Which region does a constant
scrutinee take" is not a second "taken region" method: it is upstream's
`RegionBranchOpInterface::getEntrySuccessorRegions` asked with the constant
operand (`ControlFlowInterfaces.td`), which the base class answers through
`getTakenRegion` (`Regions.cpp:56-82`); that helper stays private to the
base class, and its one outside caller (`Canon/MatchPatterns.cpp:104`) asks
`getEntrySuccessorRegions`. Deleted: the `MatchLike` concept,
`rebuildMatch(Operation*)` and its internal-error default, `scrutineeOf`,
every `isa<MatchOp, MatchLitOp>` pair (each becomes `isa<MatchOpInterface>`),
the explicit template instantiations. Consumers: L02, L04, L08, L10, L11,
L12, L13, L14, L15, L17, L24.

**S3. Cells are explicit after counting: allocation is split from
construction** (ruling A4, the owner's MLIR-native pick: MLIR separates
values from memory; ODS text by L02 in `IdrOwnershipOps.td` for the cell
type and ops, by L03 in `IdrOps.td` for `idr.con`'s change; semantics by
L02; the rewrites by L13; the lowering by L07).

1. *Value stage* (before idr-rc): `idr.con` builds a constructor value, as at
   the base, less `UnitAttr:$stack`, `$holes` and `$dests`, which are
   deleted: `(ins Idr_TagAttr:$tag, Variadic<AnyType>:$fields)`, builder
   `(type, tag, fields)`. It has no token and no cell; it stays foldable. A
   hole is a field of a cell written later, memory, which only idr-trmc
   makes (`Tail/Trmc.cpp:87`), after idr-rc (`Pipeline.cpp:99,102`), when
   every con that builds a cell is one; the frontend writes none. So holes
   and their destinations live on `idr.cell.init` alone (item 5), and
   `idr.con`'s builders, accessors (`getField`/`getDest`) and syntax lose
   them. Its effects are otherwise as at the base.
2. *idr-rc's cells step* (L13, `idr.func(idr-rc-cells)`, the first of S27's
   idr-rc steps, at stage `first`) rewrites every `idr.con` for which S36's
   `buildsCell` holds into one `idr.cell.new` and one `idr.cell.init`. The
   cell ops are legal from this step on, at stage `first`. After idr-rc the
   owned verifier (L15) refuses such an `idr.con`; an unboxed sum's con and
   an atom's con stay `idr.con`.
3. *The cell type* (L02, a `TypeDef` in `IdrOwnershipOps.td`):
   `!idr.cell<box type, tag>`, printed `!idr.cell<!idr.box<!L>, @Cons>`, the
   uninitialised memory of one cell for that constructor. The parameters are
   `(::idr::BoxType box, ::idr::Tag tag)`, as everywhere else in the dialect
   a data type is a named type (`IdrTypes.td:Idr_DataType`, a `MutableType`)
   and a constructor is its tag in it, printed by name (`custom<CtorRef>`,
   as `idr.con` prints its tag). It has no grade; it is linear by type
   (`isLinearByType()` true, S10), so a cell is used exactly once, by
   `idr.cell.init`; it is not counted (`holdsReferences` and `isCounted`
   false); its verifier refuses a tag for which `buildsCell` fails, so an
   atom has no cell.
4. *Cell producers*, one op per source, each with its effect declared in ODS
   on the op (no flag decides an effect); the producer writes the cell's
   header:
   - `idr.cell.new`: a fresh heap cell
     (`Res<..., [MemAlloc<DefaultResource, 0, FullEffect>]>`), as
     `memref.alloc` (`MemRefOps.td:AllocLikeOp`);
   - `idr.cell.stack`: a cell in the frame
     (`MemAlloc<AutomaticAllocationScopeResource, 0, FullEffect>`), as
     `memref.alloca`, whose verifier requires an ancestor with
     `AutomaticAllocationScope`, which `idr.func` is. idr-rc's stack step
     (`idr-rc-stack`, L13, S27) replaces an `idr.cell.new` by it where L09's
     escape analysis proves the cell stays in its frame, before reuse and
     exclusivity are decided, so Reuses and Exclusivity see stack cells and
     the base's "stack beats reuse" priority holds. That is upstream's
     order: `promote-buffers-to-stack` turns `memref.alloc` into
     `memref.alloca` after bufferization
     (`Bufferization/Transforms/Passes.td:PromoteBuffersToStackPass`). The
     separate idr-stack pass that ran before idr-rc (`Pipeline.cpp:94`), on
     the value stage where no cell exists, is deleted. The escape analysis
     (`Analysis/Escapes.cpp`, already upstream's
     `SparseBackwardDataFlowAnalysis`) reads uses by their flow edges, which
     model references, not addresses: `idr.share` releases its operand and
     its result is "a value no flow explains" (`FlowOps.cpp:213-215`), though
     it is the same cell, and `idr.cell.init`'s result is its cell. Escapes
     follows the address itself, through `idr.share` and from a cell to its
     init's result (S11's `sourceOf` never looks through a share), or a cell
     that escapes through a share would go on the stack: a use after return.
     That is L09's obligation, with a stack fixture whose cell escapes
     through an `idr.share`;
   - `idr.cell.recycle %token`: the token's cell, or a fresh one when the
     token is null (the take of a shared box), with exactly
     `memref.realloc`'s effects (`MemRefOps.td:MemRef_ReallocOp`):
     `MemFreeAt<0, FullEffect>` on the token, whose cell is given up, and
     `MemAlloc<DefaultResource, 1, FullEffect>` on the result, which may be
     the same memory. Reuse (L13, in idr-rc's place step, reading the cached `Reuses`) replaces an
     `idr.cell.new` by it. Which cell may be recycled for which constructor
     is the Reuses analysis's decision (L10), as at the base; the op does
     not re-check it. Reuses' candidates are `idr.cell.new` ops, so a stack
     cell is never recycled and Reuses' stack tests (`Reuses.cpp:174,209`)
     go.

   Reuse and stack placement each replace one producer op by another, so the
   `idr.cell.init` that names the cell never changes: Reuse.cpp's site maps
   and Trmc's second rebuild have nothing left to track.
5. `idr.cell.init %cell (fields..., holes)`, with `$dests` as `idr.con` has
   them at the base: writes the fields of the cell's constructor into the
   cell (`MemWrite` on the cell) and consumes it; holes and destinations
   live here alone, `holes` an `Idr_HolePositions` (S17). Its fields are
   checked against the constructor by one declared constraint
   (`detail::fillsCell`, L02's S28 hunk), not a hand verifier. Its results
   are a function of the cell's type and `holes`, so it implements
   `InferTypeOpInterface`: the box at the plain grade, then
   `!idr.dest<field>` per hole. The result is not owned at creation: the
   cells step runs at stage `first`, where an owned value is refused
   (`Verify/Program.cpp:230`), and idr-rc's grades step grades it later;
   `isCompatibleReturnTypes` admits the box at the grades the later steps
   write (owned, and excl from the commit). The format prints the result
   type only when it is not the inferred one, so an owned or excl box
   round-trips; the destinations come from a directive over
   `CellInitOp::destTypes` (L03's `custom<CellDests>`): one source. The
   base's hand inference of the same types in `parseDests` (`Ops.cpp`), in
   `ConOp::build` and `ReuseOp::build`, and `verifyHoles` are deleted.
6. *Lowering* (L07): `idr.cell.new` is the runtime's allocation,
   `idr.cell.stack` an alloca, `idr.cell.recycle` the token-or-allocate branch
   (read from the base's `LowerReuse`,
   `git show HEAD:foreign/idr/lib/Conversion/Counting.cpp`), each storing
   the header; `idr.cell.init` stores the fields; `LowerCon` keeps unboxed
   sums and atoms. L08 deletes `LowerReuse`. `!idr.cell<...>` is one pointer component in S20's
   walk, so the lowering's `TypeConverter` (fed by `Layouts::components`,
   `Lower.cpp:91-97`) converts it and each cell op is a plain
   `OpConversionPattern`; `idr.cell.stack`'s slot is placed at its
   `AutomaticAllocationScope`'s entry, as a stack cell is today
   (`Cells.cpp:42-47`).
7. *Flow* (L17, `lib/IR/FlowOps.cpp`): edges for the four new ops (a recycle
   consumes its token; an init moves its fields into the cell and consumes
   the cell); `ReuseOp`'s edges are deleted.
8. *Deleted:* `ReuseOp`, `idr.con`'s `stack` attribute and every test of it,
   `idr.con`'s `holes`, `$dests`, `custom<Dests>` and `getDest`, the
   holes tests of `Specialize/Patterns.cpp:37,43`,
   `tail::Built` and its visits, `isa<ConOp, ReuseOp>` pairs, Reuse.cpp's two

Consumers: L03 (`Verify/Program.cpp`; `Ops.cpp`'s `Fields`, `CellResult`

**S4. Taking a value apart: `idr.take` and `idr.unpack`, and atoms** (L02,
ruling A6 (mlir-5); `DataType::isAtom` by L04). The three operand kinds of
the base's one `idr.take` (a cell, an unboxed sum, an atom) are two
meanings, each its own op with its own declared effects, chosen by S36's
`buildsCell(type, tag)`, the one place they meet (essential: a cell or
none). `idr.take %box @C -> (token, fields...)` is the take of a cell (a box
whose constructor is not an atom): `(outs Idr_OwnedToken:$token,
Variadic<AnyType>:$fields)`, the token always there and no segment sizes,
`MemRead, MemWrite, MemFree` on the box as at the base. `idr.unpack %v @C ->
(fields...)` is the take of a value with no cell of its own (an unboxed
sum's slots; an atom, no results): `Idr_ConsumesOnly`, so its consumption
is declared and an atom's unpack, which has no result, is never erased as
dead; no effect on a cell. Each implements `InferTypeOpInterface`, each
field at `fieldType(value, field)`, owned where it holds references, and
`isCompatibleReturnTypes` admits the excl grade the commit writes later;
each builder is `(value, tag)`, and each refuses the other's operand
(`idr.take` of an unboxed sum or an atom does not verify).
`::idr::DataType::isAtom(::idr::Tag) const` (L04, `IdrTypes.td`/`Types.cpp`):
no fields and not a memo sum's state. A nullary boxed `idr.con` lowers to the
static atom cell (L07), so no heap cell is made that a take would not free.
Lowering: `LowerTake` keeps the cell's body (L08), `LowerUnpack` the
projection (L07). Deleted: the hand `getToken`/`getFields` and their
`drop_front`, `taken`, `movedField`, the three hand result lists, the
`Optional` token and `AttrSizedResultSegments`, every other spelling of
token presence (ten sites: each is the op it is), `LowerTake`'s two type
branches, the divergent box tests in Stack, Reshape and Reuses. Consumers:
L03, L07, L08, L10, L12, L13, L14, L15, L17 (`FlowOps.cpp`: unpack's
edges), L20 (`SyntaxSamples.idr`: `takeOp`, `unpackOp`).

**S11. A value's structural source** (L04, `Grades.h`; the trait's ODS text
by L05 in `IdrBase.td`). `::idr::Source sourceOf(::mlir::Value)` returns
`std::variant<Made, Same, Field>`: `Same{Value}` for the result of an op
with the trait `Idr_SameValue` (operand 0) and for a default region's
argument (S2, by our own rule: the match declares no predecessor for it);
`Field{Value scrutinee, Tag, unsigned index}` for `idr.field`, a memo part
included, and a case region's argument; `Made` otherwise. With S1's
`knownTag`. `Idr_SameValue` (`def Idr_SameValue : NativeOpTrait<"SameValue">
{ let cppNamespace = "::idr"; }`, its C++ class an empty `TraitBase` in
L04's S28 hunk) marks a grade op whose result is its operand's value, its
identity and exclusivity kept; L02 attaches it to `idr.borrow`,
`idr.lin.enter` and `idr.lin.use`. `idr.share` lacks it: a share carries its
operand (`ResultCarriesOperand`) but forgets exclusivity, so following it

its own extras; Exclusivity keeps its own edge search. Consumers: L02, L09
(BindingTimes, which now looks through grade ops), L10 (IdentitiesRecord,

**S36. Whether a constructor has a cell** (L02, `IR/Ownership.h`). `bool
idr::buildsCell(mlir::Type type, idr::Tag tag)`: a value of `type`, at any
grade, is a box and constructor `tag` is not an atom (`isBoxed(type) &&
!dataTypeOf(type).isAtom(tag)`, defined in `OpsOwnership.cpp`). It is the
one place the two cases meet: a con for which it holds becomes
`idr.cell.new` and `idr.cell.init` in idr-rc's cells step and its take is
`idr.take`; any other con stays `idr.con` and its take is `idr.unpack` (S3,
S4); `!idr.cell`'s verifier requires it. Testing at any grade fixes §7's
linear-box bug (`Stack.cpp:73` tests `isa<BoxType>` alone). Consumers: L07
(`LowerCon` keeps the others), L13 (the cells and stack steps), L15 (the
owned verifier refuses an `idr.con` for which it holds after idr-rc).

## Common obligations (every lane)

- **The packet is the contract.** `proposals/0004-representation/README.md`
  (§1 invariants, §2 rules, §3 findings, §4 shared contracts, §7 bugs, §9
  decisions) and `ownership.json` decide; this dispatch quotes what you
  need. AGENTS.md binds as always. Where live source contradicts the packet,
  report the exact evidence to the coordinator and keep working on the rest;
  do not redesign.
- **Write only your exclusive files.** Re-read a file immediately before
  editing it; other lanes are writing nearby files at the same time. Never
  revert, reformat or "fix" a change you did not make. A hub file (any
  `CMakeLists.txt`, `*.ipkg`, `Makefile`, `tools/**`, `PINS.md`,
  `upstream/**`, `tests/spec/**`, `tests/ACCEPTANCE.md`) and the generated
  `compiler/src/IdrisMLIR/{Dialect,Syntax,Encoding}/**` are the
  coordinator's: put the exact text you need in your handoff.
- **Hard cutover, zero backwards compatibility (the owner's rule).** The new
  representation replaces the old one in the same change, everywhere in your
  writes: no shim, alias, re-export, deprecated name, wrapper keeping an old
  signature, dual code path, fallback to the old form, compatibility flag,
  "legacy" branch, or comment promising a later removal. Old textual IR,
  bytecode, option names and layouts are not kept readable; fixtures you own
  are rewritten to the new form. A consumer outside your writes is named in
  your handoff for its owner to cut over, never served by a bridge you keep.
- **Map onto MLIR's grain (the owner's rule, 2026-10-17: "don't be afraid to
  churn massive portions of the codebase to be representation first to map
  well onto mlir").** Read the skill's section "Map onto MLIR's grain"
  before your first C++ or ODS edit. One op per semantics: never an optional
  operand, unit attribute or enum that switches an op's meaning, effects or
  valid states. A shared shape is an interface. Effects, constraints, result
  types, assembly formats, properties, folders and simple rewrites are
  declared in ODS. Values and memory live at different levels, lowered
  progressively. Cached analyses go through the `AnalysisManager`, dataflow
  through `DataFlowSolver`, lowering through `TypeConverter` and the
  conversion framework, symbols through `SymbolTable`, diagnostics through
  `emitError`, driver failures through `llvm::Error`, unreachable code
  through `ub`. Prefer deleting our C++ an upstream mechanism replaces to
  adding any; a new C++ abstraction says in its comment why no upstream
  mechanism fits.
- **Program with the types (Idris 2, after Brady; the owner's rule).** Read
  `.claude/skills/representation-first/SKILL.md`, the section "Program with
  the types: Idris 2, not Haskell", before your first Idris edit: index the
  invariant; decide with evidence, never a `Bool`; keep proofs and indices at
  quantity 0; return the value with what was learned; one record, never
  parallel lists; `List1` where empty would be an error; views and `with`.
  `List` is for sequential consumption only (the owner, 2026-10-17): a
  position is a `Vect n`/`Fin n` or, where it is hot and mutated, base's
  `Data.IOArray`; a key is a `SortedMap`; repeated appends are a
  `SnocList`; data that belong together are one record, never lists matched
  by position. No blanket rewrite: change a `List` where it is indexed,
  keyed, appended to in a loop or paired by position, in code your findings
  touch. `libs/mlir-array`'s linear arrays are runtime `%extern`s, so code
  the stock host runs (the frontend, `libs/`, the test machinery) never uses
  them. The C++ has its analogue: a `std::variant` or an enum where flags would
  combine, a type that carries a checked fact instead of a re-check, no
  sentinel and no null where a case is meant.
- **Two hosts, forever.** Idris you write (frontend, `libs/`, test machinery)
  must build with the stock Idris on Chez and with idris-mlir: stay inside
  the subset idris-mlir compiles (no escape hatch, no `%foreign`, no
  megamorphic recursion; `tests/reject/` shows the rules).
- **Every number needs authority**: a published default, a measurement, or a
  stated derivation in a comment; otherwise it is debt and the comment says
  so. Never delete an existing protective cap.
- **Verification policy (this machine).** No LLVM is built here: never
  `make bootstrap`, `tools/bootstrap.sh`, `make build`, `make test*`,
  `make self` or `make compile`. Shared build state is the coordinator's
  while lanes run, so never run `make typecheck` (or any `typecheck-*`
  part), `make check`, `make fork`, `make frontend`, `make libs`,
  `make runner`, or `tools/dialects.sh generate`.
  - **C++ lanes** do not compile during the swarm: the generated headers
    every unit includes come from every lane's ODS at once. Your evidence is
    the source: each selected representation built, each named predecessor
    gone (a `grep` for every deleted name finds nothing in your files), each
    consumer of yours adapted. The coordinator's `make typecheck` after
    integration is the gate, and its errors in your files come back to you
    as a repair dispatch.
  - **Idris lanes** work in a private copy, never the live tree:
    `mkdir -p /tmp/0004-<lane> && git -C /Users/bjorn/Documents/idris-mlir archive HEAD compiler tests libs | tar -x -C /tmp/0004-<lane>/`
    (HEAD is this packet's base at dispatch), then apply your own edits
    there as you make them in the tree. Build the frontend with the pinned
    Idris on Chez as `/tmp/0003c-gate/front.sh` does (read it), against the
    fork `make typecheck` installed (`build/idris2-host`), and run it over
    `tests/programs`, `tests/accept` and `tests/reject` with
    `/tmp/0003c-gate/scripts/runtest.sh` (read it) into
    `/tmp/0004-<lane>/out`, comparing status, stdout, stderr and Core with
    the base frontend built the same way in `/tmp/0004-<lane>/base`. Code
    that reads a generated module this wave changes (S0) is written against
    §4's names and built only at integration; say which in your handoff.
  - **The runtime lane** builds with the host clang and runs the runtime's
    property programs as `tests/toolchain` and 0002 §11 describe.
  - Every new or changed test this machine cannot run carries a first-line
    `NEEDS-ACCEPTANCE:` mark saying what to confirm.
- **Tests.** A brittle test is deleted, never restated. A test states a
  contract (a verifier refusal, a property, an output), never an SSA name or
  an op order the change does not decide. Each §7 bug you own gets the
  discriminating fixture the README names.
- **No commits, no pushes, no git writes.** The coordinator integrates.
- **Handoff** (your final message, compact): changed paths, each mapped to an
  obligation; for each finding, its representation line (the state made
  unrepresentable, the check moved to a boundary, the branch deleted, or why
  a case is essential) and a count of branches, guards and checks removed;
  contracts supplied; consumer adaptations made and any listed adaptation
  that was a false match; hub text the coordinator must apply; checks
  actually run with their results, or NotRun; unresolved seams, each with
  its evidence.

## Binding rules (verbatim, every dispatch)

1. Do exactly the assigned obligations and the necessary consumer adaptations within the exclusive write set. Every changed hunk, new file, dependency or abstraction must map to a named obligation. If the contract cannot be completed within those writes, report the exact missing seam; do not silently widen scope.
2. Add no unsolicited features, frameworks, generic helpers, configuration knobs, retries, telemetry, documentation, dependencies, formatting sweeps or neighboring cleanup. Elegance means completing the selected representation and deleting its named predecessor, not opening another project.
3. Do not be afraid to duplicate reading, investigation, reasoning or small, packet-local, non-authoritative glue. Do not wait for a sibling just to avoid that duplication, and do not introduce a shared helper that creates a false dependency. Reuse repairs that have already landed; duplicated investigation does not mean rebuilding working mechanisms.
4. Authoritative schemas, vocabularies, identities and business facts still have exactly one owner. Never duplicate them, create competing implementations or write concurrently to another owner's file. Duplicate effort is allowed; duplicate authority and overlapping writes are not.
5. Finish the bounded deliverable, report changed paths against obligations, the checks actually run and any unresolved seams, then return control. Do not roam into another packet, manufacture work to keep up the headcount, or build a reporting or coordination platform.
6. User steering goes through the coordinator, into the affected packet only. The coordinator corrects an architectural contradiction in the canonical contract and re-dispatches the affected lane. No lane stops for it.
